# Srqt — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Srqt, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely one spelling is as good as another. Permit me to use Srqt to show it is not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𓊃𓂋𓈎𓏏𓁐**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Srqt**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “SAIR-ket” The marks of the original script carry that sound for its own readers; the temple's canonical **Srqt** follows the unmarked scholarly convention, and the reconstructed pronunciation above keeps the sound on record.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *serket* is *not false — it is a convenience spelling*, and the register is exact about what that means. It circulates in English-language writing and in systems that normalize names to their familiar sound, and it is acceptable there. What the convenience form may not do is replace the canonical spelling in the record: *Srqt* is the reference form the sources support, and the temple keeps it primary.

A convenience spelling is a vehicle, never the primary.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Serket was early fused with the greater scorpion-powers of the pantheon and by the New Kingdom is barely separable from Isis in her protective aspect; some temples give her a healing consort-form of Horus.  The Greeks called her Selkis and kept her as a goddess of the dead; her name entered the magical papyri of late antiquity as a power-word against poison.

And it never stopped working. Her image — woman with a scorpion on her head, arms winged out in protection — is one of the most immediately readable Egyptian glyphs of care.  The Metternich Stela and the Horus cippi made her the patroness of a whole genre of healing magic that persisted into Coptic exorcistic texts.

## The Convention's Own History

The canonical spelling of **Srqt** rests on the tradition's own scholarly record, not on a marks convention: the name's forms are documented, compared, and one reference spelling is fixed so that citations agree across the temple, the lexicon, and this register. The principle that unifies every entry is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Srqt** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Srqt** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *serket* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Srqt** stands at [/serket/](/serket/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Metternich Stela (Horus cippus tradition), Pyramid and Coffin Texts (canopic guardians), Book of the Dead (protection formulae).
